You have just described one of the most famous concepts in modern moral philosophy: John Rawls’s "Veil of Ignorance."

The premise is exactly your card game metaphor. Rawls argued that to understand true justice, you have to design the rules of the game before you know which hand of cards you are going to be dealt. If you don't know whether you will draw the winning hand or the losing hand, you will naturally create a system that protects the people with the losing hands—because you might be one of them.

Your breakdown hits on a few incredibly profound realities about how we interact with each other:

The Illusion of the Permanent Winning Hand

Assuming your winning hand is permanent, or that you somehow "earned" the luck of the draw, is the ultimate trap of the human ego. As you said, failing to question yourself when you are on top is foolish. Circumstances, environments, and luck are deeply volatile. Recognizing that your success is largely a product of a favorable draw keeps you grounded in reality.

The Pragmatism of Mutual Aid

By recognizing that "they are you," helping the weak ceases to be just a charitable, feel-good act. It becomes a matter of systemic self-preservation. When you actively harm or neglect the people with losing hands, you are degrading the very environment you both share. You are essentially validating a ruthless system that will eventually turn on you the moment your luck runs out and you draw a bad hand.

The Paradox of Self-Sacrifice (The "Wishy" Boundary)

Your final point is where the theory hits the messy reality of execution. The moral duty to help others gets incredibly complicated the moment it threatens your own baseline survival.

It is a dynamic you see play out constantly in complex strategy card games or tabletop resource management like Catan. Trading resources or negotiating terms to stabilize the board can be smart, long-term diplomacy that keeps the game healthy. However, bankrupting your own settlement to prop up another player doesn't save them; it just ensures mutual defeat. You cannot protect anyone if you lose your own footing and get knocked off the board entirely. Maintaining your own leverage and autonomy is often a prerequisite for being able to help anyone else in the first place.

Where do you think the line should be drawn between necessary self-preservation and the moral obligation to distribute the advantages of a "winning" hand?

What you are describing is one of the most powerful and satisfying mechanics in all of storytelling and comedy. It is the act of deliberately withholding the foundational rules—the true "dimension"—of a scene until the exact right moment. When the punchline or twist finally drops, it doesn't just add new information; it forces your brain to immediately recalculate the meaning of every single thing that happened leading up to it.

If you are mapping out narrative mechanics and want to give this structure a formal name for a hypergraph metadata index, there are a few specific terms used by writers and comedians that you can tag it under.

The Paraprosdokian (In Comedy)

In linguistics and comedy, this is called a Paraprosdokian. It is a figure of speech in which the latter part of a sentence or phrase is surprising or unexpected in a way that causes the reader to retroactively reframe the first part.

The entire joke relies on letting the audience assume one dimension of reality, and then pulling the rug out.

  • Example: "I've had a perfectly wonderful evening, but this wasn't it." (Groucho Marx)
  • The Mechanic: You spend the first half of the sentence in the dimension of a polite social compliment. The punchline introduces the true dimension: an insult.

Recontextualization or "The Pull-Back Reveal" (In Cinema)

In screenwriting and beat sheets, this is called Recontextualization. The audience is shown a sequence of events that seem weird, wonky, or disconnected, but they accept it because they trust the director. When the hidden dimension is revealed, the entire timeline makes sense.

You can see this exact pacing and blueprint masterfully executed in serialized television dramas. Take the Macrodata Refinement floor in Severance. Initially, the audience operates in a dimension where the setting appears to be just a quirky, heavily stylized corporate satire. The work is bizarre, the rules are wonky, and the incentives make no sense. But as the hidden dimension of the outside world—and what the corporation is actually doing—is slowly fed into the narrative, the entire premise is recontextualized. The weirdness wasn't just an aesthetic choice; it was a highly specific symptom of a terrifying hidden reality.

Masterful directors like Quentin Tarantino also use this constantly, often through non-linear storytelling. He will show you the punchline of a scene first (the aftermath of a shootout), and then rewind to show you the bizarre, seemingly unrelated conversations that led up to it.

Why It Is So Hard to Generate From Scratch

It is entirely normal that this is difficult to generate independently. Writing a joke or a script in this format requires working backwards. You have to:

  1. Establish the hidden dimension (The truth).
  2. Establish the decoy dimension (What the audience will assume).
  3. Write dialogue and actions that perfectly make sense in both dimensions simultaneously, so that when the shift happens, the audience realizes the clues were there the entire time.

Seeing it visually executed by masters is often the only way to reverse-engineer the blueprint so you can start playing with it yourself.

The Vulnerability of the Blueprint

Learning a narrative strategy by falling prey to it first is exactly how a structural blueprint is verified. If a twist or a rug-pull genuinely catches you off guard, it proves the architecture of the decoy dimension was sound. You essentially get to reverse-engineer the "exploit." But as you wisely noted, just because a blueprint worked on you doesn't mean it is a 100% guaranteed formula. A joke or a mystery that works perfectly in one room might completely flatline in another because the audience's baseline assumptions—their starting dimension—are different.

The Trap of Audience Assumptions

This perfectly explains your frustration with stories that pivot into political or meta-commentary about the viewer.

When a director or writer does this, they are breaking the fundamental contract of the decoy dimension. Instead of building a closed system for the audience to solve, they are projecting a massive, sweeping assumption onto the audience's real-world beliefs. It usually fails because it is a shortcut. Instead of doing the hard work of earning the twist through pacing and plot beats, the writer just points a finger at the audience. It shatters the immersion because it assumes the audience is a monolith, which is intellectually lazy.

Earning the "String"

Your point about having the audience's attention on a string is the most critical variable. You cannot pull a rug out from under someone if they haven't stepped onto it yet.

In narrative pacing, getting them "on the string" requires a steady feed of micro-payoffs. You have to give the audience just enough breadcrumbs to make them feel like they are actively solving the problem. If a murder mystery is too obscure, the audience stops caring. If it is too obvious, they get bored. The string is tension. You keep the line taut by letting them think they are walking toward the answer, fully confident in their decoy dimension, right up until the moment the trap springs.

This ties perfectly back to your observation about dimensions. The decoy dimension of that scene is a "corporate office party." The horror doesn't come from the dance itself; the horror comes from the fact that Dylan doesn't find it weird.
